# `energyml` - command reference

<!-- Generated by `energyml cli-reference` from the command definitions; do not edit by hand. `energyml cli-reference --out <file>` writes it, `--check` fails when it is stale. -->

Built with the features: `hdf5`, `png`. How each command is used, with examples, is in [`cli.md`](cli.md); this page is every option of every command, as `--help` prints it.

## Commands

- [`energyml list`](#energyml-list) - List the objects an EPC holds
- [`energyml check`](#energyml-check) - Report everything wrong with an EPC: the package, the objects, the references
- [`energyml show`](#energyml-show) - Print one object, as XML or JSON
- [`energyml arrays`](#energyml-arrays) - List the external arrays the objects point at, and the files holding them
- [`energyml properties`](#energyml-properties) - List the properties: what they hang on, what kind they are, how many values
- [`energyml colors`](#energyml-colors) - Resolve the colour of every object, saying which level it came from
- [`energyml tables`](#energyml-tables) - Print the lookup tables: their columns, their keys, and their rows
- [`energyml wells`](#energyml-wells) - Write a package's wellbores as a table - one row per node, the discrete values resolved
- [`energyml series`](#energyml-series) - Read a log, a time series, a flow test or production periods as series: the index, the channels, what is absent or flagged, and why a reading is refused
- [`energyml geometry`](#energyml-geometry) - Evaluate the geometry of every representation: points, topology, CRS
- [`energyml export`](#energyml-export) - Write representations out to an interchange format
- [`energyml types`](#energyml-types) - List the schema types this build can read
- [`energyml docs`](#energyml-docs) - Write the model's documentation as JSON - every type, field and value, with the `xsd:documentation`, one file per (package, version)
- [`energyml repair`](#energyml-repair) - Work on the parts no parser will touch: list them, take their bytes out, put repaired bytes back
- [`energyml graph`](#energyml-graph) - Export the reference graph, for something else to draw
- [`energyml h5`](#energyml-h5) - Say where each array's numbers really are, and fix the package to agree
- [`energyml relabel`](#energyml-relabel) - Correct the schema version a package's parts declare, without reading what they hold
- [`energyml extract`](#energyml-extract) - Cut a package down to a chosen set of objects, and say what that cost
- [`energyml rename`](#energyml-rename) - Rename the external data file a package points at - the fields, the relationships and the file itself, or refuse
- [`energyml sources`](#energyml-sources) - List the public APIs this build can query, and what each one offers
- [`energyml fetch`](#energyml-fetch) - Quote - and then harvest - a query against one of them
- [`energyml rules`](#energyml-rules) - List the rules: the house rules of this library, where the specification is silent
- [`energyml profile`](#energyml-profile) - Project the wells of a package on a drawn track: which fall in the band, where along it, on which side
- [`energyml select`](#energyml-select) - Select the objects of a package that fall in a region drawn by outer and inner rings: a list of uuids or uris to chain into an operation
- [`energyml import`](#energyml-import) - Read a GeoJSON and write the EnergyML objects it describes
- [`energyml create`](#energyml-create) - Create objects through one door: list what an input allows, plan it, write it
- [`energyml terrain`](#energyml-terrain) - A digital elevation model from a catalogue source, written as a 2D grid - the quote without `--out`

## `energyml`

```text
Command-line tool to inspect and validate EnergyML data stores (EPC files today).

Usage: energyml [OPTIONS] <COMMAND>

Commands:
  list        List the objects an EPC holds
  check       Report everything wrong with an EPC: the package, the objects, the references
  show        Print one object, as XML or JSON
  arrays      List the external arrays the objects point at, and the files holding them
  properties  List the properties: what they hang on, what kind they are, how many values
  colors      Resolve the colour of every object, saying which level it came from
  tables      Print the lookup tables: their columns, their keys, and their rows
  wells       Write a package's wellbores as a table - one row per node, the discrete values resolved
  series      Read a log, a time series, a flow test or production periods as series: the index, the channels, what is absent or flagged, and why a reading is refused
  geometry    Evaluate the geometry of every representation: points, topology, CRS
  export      Write representations out to an interchange format
  types       List the schema types this build can read
  docs        Write the model's documentation as JSON - every type, field and value, with the `xsd:documentation`, one file per (package, version)
  repair      Work on the parts no parser will touch: list them, take their bytes out, put repaired bytes back
  graph       Export the reference graph, for something else to draw
  h5          Say where each array's numbers really are, and fix the package to agree
  relabel     Correct the schema version a package's parts declare, without reading what they hold
  extract     Cut a package down to a chosen set of objects, and say what that cost
  rename      Rename the external data file a package points at - the fields, the relationships and the file itself, or refuse
  sources     List the public APIs this build can query, and what each one offers
  fetch       Quote - and then harvest - a query against one of them
  rules       List the rules: the house rules of this library, where the specification is silent
  profile     Project the wells of a package on a drawn track: which fall in the band, where along it, on which side
  select      Select the objects of a package that fall in a region drawn by outer and inner rings: a list of uuids or uris to chain into an operation
  import      Read a GeoJSON and write the EnergyML objects it describes
  create      Create objects through one door: list what an input allows, plan it, write it
  terrain     A digital elevation model from a catalogue source, written as a 2D grid - the quote without `--out`
  help        Print this message or the help of the given subcommand(s)

Options:
      --lenient
          Read parts that break the schema instead of refusing them.
          
          Two kinds of defect are read past. An absent required element comes back as its default; a value that is *there* and unreadable - a word outside a closed enumeration, a number that is not a number, an undefined entity, an `xsi:type` naming an unknown subtype of a concrete base - is replaced, and the string that was in the file is reported.
          
          Every one of them is reported. Use it to get at the contents of a package whose producer wrote something wrong; do not use it for anything that will be written back, since what comes out is not what the document said.
          
          Still refused in both modes: malformed XML, bad encoding, and an `xsi:type` on a purely abstract choice - there is nothing to fall back to there.

      --strict
          Refuse a part that omits something the schema requires.
          
          By default an absent required element is filled with its default and reported, because refusing costs every field the part *did* carry - a package whose producer left out `Citation.Originator` is otherwise unreadable in its entirety, geometry included.
          
          Use this when the objects will be **written back**: read tolerantly, they hold values nobody wrote, and saving puts those on disk.

      --h5 <[NAME=]PATH>
          An HDF5 file to read arrays from, whatever the package says.
          
          Repeatable, and **the name is optional**:
          
          - `--h5 path/to/data.h5` offers the file without naming it. Offers are opened in the order given and the first that holds the dataset wins. - `--h5 model.h5=path/to/renamed.h5` pins a path to the name the document uses, for when you know which name is wrong.
          
          The name is optional because the whole point is not having to open a `.rels` in a text editor to find out what your file used to be called. A file that was renamed still holds every number it held before.
          
          What is offered is tried **before** what the package names, since offering one is an explicit instruction and people offer them precisely when the package is wrong. Anything read from somewhere the document did not point at is reported.

      --log <FILTER>
          Show what the operations are doing, on stderr: `info`, `debug`, or a filter such as `energyml_build=debug,energyml_storage=info`.
          
          Nothing is shown by default. The same as the `ENERGYML_LOG` environment variable, which this flag overrides. Spans say how long each step took (`time.busy`). stdout is never touched, so a script reading a result is not disturbed.

      --log-format <FORMAT>
          How `--log` writes a line: `text` (default) or `json`, one object per line. Overrides `ENERGYML_LOG_FORMAT`
          
          [possible values: text, json]

  -h, --help
          Print help (see a summary with '-h')

  -V, --version
          Print version
```

## `energyml check`

```text
Report everything wrong with an EPC: the package, the objects, the references

Usage: energyml check [OPTIONS] <FILE>

Arguments:
  <FILE>
          The EPC file

Options:
      --errors-only
          Only report errors - no warnings, no notes

      --no-schema
          Skip schema validation of the objects, which is the slow part

      --rules <FILE>
          A business rule set, as JSON - **added to** the shipped one.
          
          Added rather than substituted: a house rule and a rule of the standard answer different questions, and a file that silenced the technical reference guide's associations by mentioning one rule of its own would be a surprising way to lose a check.

      --no-rules
          Do not run the business rules at all

      --max <N>
          Stop listing after this many findings per section
          
          [default: 50]

      --lenient
          Read parts that break the schema instead of refusing them.
          
          Two kinds of defect are read past. An absent required element comes back as its default; a value that is *there* and unreadable - a word outside a closed enumeration, a number that is not a number, an undefined entity, an `xsi:type` naming an unknown subtype of a concrete base - is replaced, and the string that was in the file is reported.
          
          Every one of them is reported. Use it to get at the contents of a package whose producer wrote something wrong; do not use it for anything that will be written back, since what comes out is not what the document said.
          
          Still refused in both modes: malformed XML, bad encoding, and an `xsi:type` on a purely abstract choice - there is nothing to fall back to there.

      --strict
          Refuse a part that omits something the schema requires.
          
          By default an absent required element is filled with its default and reported, because refusing costs every field the part *did* carry - a package whose producer left out `Citation.Originator` is otherwise unreadable in its entirety, geometry included.
          
          Use this when the objects will be **written back**: read tolerantly, they hold values nobody wrote, and saving puts those on disk.

      --h5 <[NAME=]PATH>
          An HDF5 file to read arrays from, whatever the package says.
          
          Repeatable, and **the name is optional**:
          
          - `--h5 path/to/data.h5` offers the file without naming it. Offers are opened in the order given and the first that holds the dataset wins. - `--h5 model.h5=path/to/renamed.h5` pins a path to the name the document uses, for when you know which name is wrong.
          
          The name is optional because the whole point is not having to open a `.rels` in a text editor to find out what your file used to be called. A file that was renamed still holds every number it held before.
          
          What is offered is tried **before** what the package names, since offering one is an explicit instruction and people offer them precisely when the package is wrong. Anything read from somewhere the document did not point at is reported.

      --log <FILTER>
          Show what the operations are doing, on stderr: `info`, `debug`, or a filter such as `energyml_build=debug,energyml_storage=info`.
          
          Nothing is shown by default. The same as the `ENERGYML_LOG` environment variable, which this flag overrides. Spans say how long each step took (`time.busy`). stdout is never touched, so a script reading a result is not disturbed.

      --log-format <FORMAT>
          How `--log` writes a line: `text` (default) or `json`, one object per line. Overrides `ENERGYML_LOG_FORMAT`
          
          [possible values: text, json]

  -h, --help
          Print help (see a summary with '-h')
```

## `energyml show`

```text
Print one object, as XML or JSON

## `energyml arrays`

```text
List the external arrays the objects point at, and the files holding them

Usage: energyml arrays [OPTIONS] <FILE>

Arguments:
  <FILE>
          The EPC file

Options:
      --summary
          Group by file instead of listing every pointer

      --values [<N>]
          Read each array and print its shape, element type and first values.
          
          Needs a backend: build with `--features hdf5`, or the reads report the missing capability.

          Read parts that break the schema instead of refusing them.

## `energyml properties`

```text
List the properties: what they hang on, what kind they are, how many values

Usage: energyml properties [OPTIONS] <FILE>

Arguments:
  <FILE>
          The EPC file

Options:
      --representation <UUID>
          Only properties hanging on this representation (uuid)

      --check
          Read the values, and report where their count contradicts the document.
          
          Needs a backend: build with `--features hdf5`, or the reads report the missing capability.

      --dictionary <FILE>
          A `PropertyKindDictionary` XML file, replacing the built-in one.
          
          The build carries the Energistics eml 2.3 dictionary; pass a newer one, or a company one, to resolve kinds this build does not know.

          Read parts that break the schema instead of refusing them.

## `energyml colors`

```text
Resolve the colour of every object, saying which level it came from

Usage: energyml colors [OPTIONS] <FILE>

Arguments:
  <FILE>
          The EPC file

Options:
      --object <UUID>
          Only this object (uuid)

      --no-inherit
          Do not look at the interpretation and the feature.
          
          Nothing in the standard says a colour is inherited; this repository decided it is, in a fallback chain. This switch turns that off and leaves only what each object carries itself.

      --viewer <KIND>
          Which viewer the colours are for: `3d` (default), `base map`, `section`, `well correlation`.
          
          An entry meant for another viewer is skipped rather than drawn.
          
          [default: 3d]

      --lenient
          Read parts that break the schema instead of refusing them.
          
          Two kinds of defect are read past. An absent required element comes back as its default; a value that is *there* and unreadable - a word outside a closed enumeration, a number that is not a number, an undefined entity, an `xsi:type` naming an unknown subtype of a concrete base - is replaced, and the string that was in the file is reported.
          
          Every one of them is reported. Use it to get at the contents of a package whose producer wrote something wrong; do not use it for anything that will be written back, since what comes out is not what the document said.

          [possible values: text, json]

  -h, --help
          Print help (see a summary with '-h')
```

## `energyml tables`

```text
Print the lookup tables: their columns, their keys, and their rows

Usage: energyml tables [OPTIONS] <FILE>

Arguments:
  <FILE>
          The EPC file

Options:
      --rows <N>
          Print this many rows of each table.
          
          Needs a backend for a column-based table, whose values live in an external file; a RESQML 2.0.1 lookup is inline and needs none.
          
          [default: 10]

      --lenient
          Read parts that break the schema instead of refusing them.
          
          Two kinds of defect are read past. An absent required element comes back as its default; a value that is *there* and unreadable - a word outside a closed enumeration, a number that is not a number, an undefined entity, an `xsi:type` naming an unknown subtype of a concrete base - is replaced, and the string that was in the file is reported.

## `energyml export`

```text
Write representations out to an interchange format

Usage: energyml export [OPTIONS] <FILE>

Arguments:
  <FILE>
          The EPC file

Options:
      --format <FORMAT>
          Which format. `--list` shows what this build offers
          
          [default: obj]

  -o, --out <PATH>
          Where to write. A directory gets one file per representation; a file gets all of them together, where the format allows it

      --filter <SUBSTRING>
          Only representations whose type name contains this, case-insensitively

      --metadata <FILE>
          A JSON file of key → dotted path, added to every object's metadata.
          
          A path may cross references: `RepresentedInterpretation.InterpretedFeature.Citation.Title` reads through two objects. See `energyml_domain::metadata`.

      --standard-metadata
          Use the standard metadata keys - identity plus interpretation and feature - without writing a file

      --properties
          Attach the property values to what is written.
          
          VTK gets one `PointData`/`CellData` array per property, which is what a viewer colours by; GeoJSON gets a labelled summary, since a feature has one set of properties and a property has one value per element. Off by default: it means reading every property of the package and its external arrays.
          
          Needs a backend for properties stored in HDF5: build with `--features hdf5`, or each one reports the missing capability.

      --property <UUID>
          Attach only these properties (uuid), implying `--properties`

      --properties-on <SCOPE>
          Move the values onto these elements, whatever the file hangs them on.
          
          A per-node temperature looked at on the faces, a per-cell facies looked at on the points: RESQML says where a property *is*, never where someone wants to see it. `points` and `cells` transfer; leaving this out writes each property where the file put it.
          
          The transfer is a real computation and it is named, not guessed - see `--transfer-method`.
          
          [possible values: points, cells]

      --tube <RADIUS>
          Sweep every polyline into a solid tube of this radius.
          
          A well drawn as a line is one pixel wide at any distance that shows the model. A **radius**, not a diameter - every sweep in every renderer takes a radius, and converting silently at one end of a pair of interfaces is how a well comes out twice too fat.
          
          The path is swept as it stands: the points are already the evaluated curve (`parametric.rs` evaluates a minimum-curvature well path rather than straightening it), so smoothing them again would draw a path through positions the file does not state.

      --tube-sides <N>
          How many faces go round the tube - the arity of the cross-section.
          
          Three is a triangular prism and reads as a mistake; past about sixteen nothing on screen changes and every vertex is paid for.
          
          [default: 8]

      --transfer-method <METHOD>
          How several values become one when they are moved.
          
          `average` for a measurement, and it is the default. **`majority` for a category**: the mean of facies 0 and facies 3 is 1.5, which is not a facies at all, so a discrete property averaged onto the faces paints a confident picture of a rock that is not there. `minimum` and `maximum` are there for a conservative reading of a threshold.
          
          [default: average]

      --epsg <CODE>
          Reproject into this EPSG system. `4326` is WGS 84 longitude/latitude, `3857` Web Mercator. GeoJSON needs one and defaults to 4326.
          
          The elevation is **not** converted: it stays in the vertical CRS it was written in. See `energyml_proj` for why.

      --crs-definitions <FILE>
          A JSON file of `"epsg code": "proj4 string"`, replacing the built-in definitions.
          
          Where to reach for when the built-in transformation is not the one your survey specifies - it is a single Helmert per datum, good to a few metres, and sometimes that is not good enough.

      --allow-silent-datum
          Convert even from a system whose definition states no datum.
          
          Off by default, and worth leaving off: the shift to WGS 84 is then silently skipped, which on a pre-GPS datum puts the model a hundred metres or so from where it belongs, with every coordinate still looking entirely reasonable.

      --time-equivalence <M_PER_S>
          Write time-domain objects, stating what one second of vertical travel time stands for in metres.
          
          Without it a representation in a seismic time system is **refused**, and that is the honest default: the package carries no velocity model, and RESQML puts the time kind - one-way or two-way - outside the CRS, so a real depth is half or double whatever this produces.
          
          What it buys is a mesh you can look at, with the equivalence written into the file beside the geometry. `2000` is a mid-range sediment velocity and a reasonable place to start.

      --native-crs
          Write coordinates as stored, reprojecting nothing.
          
          For GeoJSON, which is WGS 84 by definition: with this flag the file carries the native projected coordinates instead, plus the legacy `crs` member naming the EPSG code when there is one (QGIS and GDAL honour it), and objects that name no CRS at all are written too. The file is knowingly non-conformant - useful for looking at a package whose georeferencing is missing or under repair.

      --as <PATTERN=SHAPE>
          Draw these types in this form: `--as PATTERN=SHAPE`, repeatable.
          
          The pattern matches anywhere in the qualified type, case-insensitively - `Grid2d`, `resqml20.`, `IjkGridRepresentation`, or `*` for everything.
          
          The shape is `points`, `lines`, `surface`, `volume` or `auto`, or one of the two **summaries** - `outline` for the convex hull of the object as a single polygon, `centroid` for the mean of its nodes as a single point. Those two answer "where is this" rather than "what is this", and carry no property: they are what OSDU's SpatialArea and SpatialPoint ask for.
          
          Rules are tried in the order given and the first match wins, so a general rule and an exception compose in one line:
          
          --as Grid2d=surface --as '*=points'
          
          A shape an object cannot take is an **error**, not a fallback: asking for a PolylineSet as a surface fails by name, because a line is not a boundary unless it closes and RESQML states closure somewhere this build does not read.

      --list
          Print the formats this build can write, and stop

      --lenient
          Read parts that break the schema instead of refusing them.
          
          Two kinds of defect are read past. An absent required element comes back as its default; a value that is *there* and unreadable - a word outside a closed enumeration, a number that is not a number, an undefined entity, an `xsi:type` naming an unknown subtype of a concrete base - is replaced, and the string that was in the file is reported.
          
          Every one of them is reported. Use it to get at the contents of a package whose producer wrote something wrong; do not use it for anything that will be written back, since what comes out is not what the document said.
          
          Still refused in both modes: malformed XML, bad encoding, and an `xsi:type` on a purely abstract choice - there is nothing to fall back to there.

      --strict
          Refuse a part that omits something the schema requires.
          
          By default an absent required element is filled with its default and reported, because refusing costs every field the part *did* carry - a package whose producer left out `Citation.Originator` is otherwise unreadable in its entirety, geometry included.
          
          Use this when the objects will be **written back**: read tolerantly, they hold values nobody wrote, and saving puts those on disk.

      --h5 <[NAME=]PATH>
          An HDF5 file to read arrays from, whatever the package says.
          
          Repeatable, and **the name is optional**:
          
          - `--h5 path/to/data.h5` offers the file without naming it. Offers are opened in the order given and the first that holds the dataset wins. - `--h5 model.h5=path/to/renamed.h5` pins a path to the name the document uses, for when you know which name is wrong.
          
          The name is optional because the whole point is not having to open a `.rels` in a text editor to find out what your file used to be called. A file that was renamed still holds every number it held before.
          
          What is offered is tried **before** what the package names, since offering one is an explicit instruction and people offer them precisely when the package is wrong. Anything read from somewhere the document did not point at is reported.

      --log <FILTER>
          Show what the operations are doing, on stderr: `info`, `debug`, or a filter such as `energyml_build=debug,energyml_storage=info`.
          
          Nothing is shown by default. The same as the `ENERGYML_LOG` environment variable, which this flag overrides. Spans say how long each step took (`time.busy`). stdout is never touched, so a script reading a result is not disturbed.

      --log-format <FORMAT>
          How `--log` writes a line: `text` (default) or `json`, one object per line. Overrides `ENERGYML_LOG_FORMAT`
          
          [possible values: text, json]

  -h, --help
          Print help (see a summary with '-h')

## `energyml repair`

```text
Work on the parts no parser will touch: list them, take their bytes out, put repaired bytes back

Usage: energyml repair [OPTIONS] <FILE>

Arguments:
  <FILE>
          The EPC file

Options:
      --extract <DIR>
          Write every unreadable part's bytes into this directory, under its own part name. The other half of `--apply`

      --apply <DIR>
          Read a directory laid out like `--extract` wrote it, and stage each file as the part of the same name. Says, for each, whether it now parses

      --out <FILE>
          Where to write the repaired package. Without it, `--apply` reports what would happen and writes nothing

      --force
          Stage a part even when the bytes still do not parse.
          
          Off by default: a repair that made nothing better is more often a mistake than an intention, and writing it would replace a broken part with a differently broken one.

      --lenient
          Read parts that break the schema instead of refusing them.
          
          Two kinds of defect are read past. An absent required element comes back as its default; a value that is *there* and unreadable - a word outside a closed enumeration, a number that is not a number, an undefined entity, an `xsi:type` naming an unknown subtype of a concrete base - is replaced, and the string that was in the file is reported.
          
          Every one of them is reported. Use it to get at the contents of a package whose producer wrote something wrong; do not use it for anything that will be written back, since what comes out is not what the document said.
          
          Still refused in both modes: malformed XML, bad encoding, and an `xsi:type` on a purely abstract choice - there is nothing to fall back to there.

      --strict
          Refuse a part that omits something the schema requires.
          
          By default an absent required element is filled with its default and reported, because refusing costs every field the part *did* carry - a package whose producer left out `Citation.Originator` is otherwise unreadable in its entirety, geometry included.
          
          Use this when the objects will be **written back**: read tolerantly, they hold values nobody wrote, and saving puts those on disk.

      --h5 <[NAME=]PATH>
          An HDF5 file to read arrays from, whatever the package says.
          
          Repeatable, and **the name is optional**:
          
          - `--h5 path/to/data.h5` offers the file without naming it. Offers are opened in the order given and the first that holds the dataset wins. - `--h5 model.h5=path/to/renamed.h5` pins a path to the name the document uses, for when you know which name is wrong.
          
          The name is optional because the whole point is not having to open a `.rels` in a text editor to find out what your file used to be called. A file that was renamed still holds every number it held before.
          
          What is offered is tried **before** what the package names, since offering one is an explicit instruction and people offer them precisely when the package is wrong. Anything read from somewhere the document did not point at is reported.

      --log <FILTER>
          Show what the operations are doing, on stderr: `info`, `debug`, or a filter such as `energyml_build=debug,energyml_storage=info`.
          
          Nothing is shown by default. The same as the `ENERGYML_LOG` environment variable, which this flag overrides. Spans say how long each step took (`time.busy`). stdout is never touched, so a script reading a result is not disturbed.

      --log-format <FORMAT>
          How `--log` writes a line: `text` (default) or `json`, one object per line. Overrides `ENERGYML_LOG_FORMAT`
          
          [possible values: text, json]

  -h, --help
          Print help (see a summary with '-h')
```

## `energyml relabel`

```text
Correct the schema version a package's parts declare, without reading what they hold

Usage: energyml relabel [OPTIONS] --package <PACKAGE> --schema-version <VERSION> <FILE>

Arguments:
  <FILE>
          The EPC file

Options:
      --package <PACKAGE>
          Which package's parts to relabel: `resqml`, `witsml`, `prodml`, `eml`.
          
          Required, and no default. Every version in an EPC is independent - the eml parts of a RESQML package have their *own* release - so relabelling everything would declare a version for objects that never had it.

      --schema-version <VERSION>
          What to write, e.g. `2.2_dev3`.
          
          Spelled the way Energistics names the release: their own distribution calls the drop `resqml_v2.2_dev3`. The reader compares versions ignoring separator and case, so `2.2dev3` and `2.2-dev3` are read the same - this is about what the file will say, not about what can be read back.

      --from <VERSION>
          Only the parts currently on this version, e.g. `2.2`.
          
          **Required as soon as the package holds more than one**, and that is not a rare shape: an EPC may legitimately mix releases (EPC §3.2), and the reference package holds RESQML 2.0.1 objects beside 2.2 ones. Relabelling on the package name alone would declare 2.0.1 parts to be a 2.2 development drop - the exact corruption this command exists to avoid, applied by the tool instead of by the producer.

  -o, --out <FILE>
          Where to write the corrected package. Without it, nothing is written and the command reports what it would change

      --lenient
          Read parts that break the schema instead of refusing them.
          
          Two kinds of defect are read past. ```text

## `energyml fetch`

```text
Quote - and then harvest - a query against one of them

Usage: energyml fetch [OPTIONS] <PROVIDER> <COLLECTION>

Arguments:
  <PROVIDER>
          The provider, as `energyml sources` names it

  <COLLECTION>
          The collection

Options:
      --area <FILE.geojson>
          An area, as GeoJSON - **the file the map view exports**.
          
          The first polygon of the document is taken; its coordinates are WGS 84 degrees, as RFC 7946 requires, and it is the provider that knows in which order its service wants them.

      --where <NAME=VALUE>
          A condition, `name=value`. Repeatable; all of them are conjoined

      --out <FILE.json>
          Harvest, and write the response **as it is** to this file.
          
          Without it nothing is written: the command says what it would cost, which is the repository's shape - `create --plan`, `extract --dry-run`, `rename` without `--apply`.
          
          **One page per file**, numbered, as soon as there are several: each page is a whole GeoJSON document, and gluing them end to end would write a file nothing reads back.

      --read
          Read the stream entity by entity without writing anything, to see what comes

      --only <NAME,NAME>
          Keep only these properties when reading (`--read`), separated by commas. Without it, everything is kept

      --shapes-only
          Keep no property - what a preview asks for

      --page <N>
          How many entities per page
          
          [default: 1000]

      --most <N>
          A ceiling in entities. The harvest stops there, and says so

      --lenient
          Read parts that break the schema instead of refusing them.
          
          Two kinds of defect are read past. ## `energyml rules`

```text
List the rules: the house rules of this library, where the specification is silent

Usage: energyml rules [OPTIONS]

Options:
      --house
          The house rules: what this library decides where the specification is silent, ambiguous or only interpreted. (The only family there is yet.)

      --id <ID>
          One rule, in full: text, reason, references

      --anchor <ANCHOR>
          The rules that show at a place, as `kind:key` - `type:Attachment`, `type:Attachment.Md`, `view:object.colour-stack`, `finding:<id>`, `operation:attach`

      --status <STATUS>
          One status: active, designed, superseded

      --json
          The registry as JSON (every language that exists, the version)

      --lang <LANG>
          The language of the texts. A rule not translated answers in English and says so
          
          [default: en]

      --lenient
          Read parts that break the schema instead of refusing them.
          
          Two kinds of defect are read past. An absent required element comes back as its default; a value that is *there* and unreadable - a word outside a closed enumeration, a number that is not a number, an undefined entity, an `xsi:type` naming an unknown subtype of a concrete base - is replaced, and the string that was in the file is reported.
          
          Every one of them is reported. Use it to get at the contents of a package whose producer wrote something wrong; do not use it for anything that will be written back, since what comes out is not what the document said.
          
          Still refused in both modes: malformed XML, bad encoding, and an `xsi:type` on a purely abstract choice - there is nothing to fall back to there.

      --strict
          Refuse a part that omits something the schema requires.
          
          By default an absent required element is filled with its default and reported, because refusing costs every field the part *did* carry - a package whose producer left out `Citation.Originator` is otherwise unreadable in its entirety, geometry included.
          
          Use this when the objects will be **written back**: read tolerantly, they hold values nobody wrote, and saving puts those on disk.

      --h5 <[NAME=]PATH>
          An HDF5 file to read arrays from, whatever the package says.
          
          Repeatable, and **the name is optional**:
          
          - `--h5 path/to/data.h5` offers the file without naming it. Offers are opened in the order given and the first that holds the dataset wins. - `--h5 model.h5=path/to/renamed.h5` pins a path to the name the document uses, for when you know which name is wrong.
          
          The name is optional because the whole point is not having to open a `.rels` in a text editor to find out what your file used to be called. A file that was renamed still holds every number it held before.
          
          What is offered is tried **before** what the package names, since offering one is an explicit instruction and people offer them precisely when the package is wrong. Anything read from somewhere the document did not point at is reported.

      --log <FILTER>
          Show what the operations are doing, on stderr: `info`, `debug`, or a filter such as `energyml_build=debug,energyml_storage=info`.
          
          Nothing is shown by default. The same as the `ENERGYML_LOG` environment variable, which this flag overrides. Spans say how long each step took (`time.busy`). stdout is never touched, so a script reading a result is not disturbed.

      --log-format <FORMAT>
          How `--log` writes a line: `text` (default) or `json`, one object per line. Overrides `ENERGYML_LOG_FORMAT`
          
          [possible values: text, json]

  -h, --help
          Print help (see a summary with '-h')
```

## `energyml profile`

```text
Project the wells of a package on a drawn track: which fall in the band, where along it, on which side

Usage: energyml profile [OPTIONS] <FILE>

Arguments:
  <FILE>
          The EPC file - the section's first package, `s1`

Options:
      --also <FILE.epc>
          With `--svg`: another package, `s2`, `s3`… in the order given. Its wells and surfaces are cut along the same sections and drawn in the same drawing, in the first package's system

      --track <FILE.geojson|x,y;x,y>
          The track: a GeoJSON file (a LineString, a Feature or a collection whose first line is used) or the vertices inline, `x,y;x,y;…`. In the placement's unit

      --left <METRES>
          Width kept on the left of the track, read in the direction it was drawn

      --right <METRES>
          Width kept on the right of the track

      --from-svg <FILE.svg>
          Draw again the section view this SVG holds, from what its metadata says it was made of, over the packages given (`FILE` is `s1`, `--also` the next) - into `--svg`, and `--png`. On the same packages, the same bytes

      --placement <PLACEMENT>
          The coordinates of the track: `projected` (the CRS as it stands), `metres` (its horizontal unit taken to metres) or `local`
          
          [default: projected]

      --well <URI|UUID>
          Which wells, by uri or uuid. Left out, every trajectory of the package - with `--svg`, every trajectory and frame of every package; given, each goes to the package that holds it

      --arc-step <ARC_STEP>
          The angle, in degrees, a rounded outer turn of the band is cut at
          
          [default: 10]

      --json
          Print the answer as JSON, with the band

      --svg <FILE.svg>
          Draw the section view as SVG into this file - wells and surfaces, the same drawing the front end shows

      --surface <URI>
          With `--svg`: a surface to cut, by uri, in whichever package holds it. Left out, every surface and grid of every package a section cuts (triangulated, 2D grids, IJK grids)

      --cross-every <METRES>
          With `--svg`: a cross section every this many metres along the track

      --cross-count <N>
          With `--svg`: this many cross sections, spread along the track

      --cross-length <METRES>
          With `--svg`: a cross section's length on each side of the track
          
          [default: 200]

      --cross-width <METRES>
          With `--svg`: a cross section's corridor on each side, for its wells
          
          [default: 50]

      --draw <DRAW>
          With `--svg`: what to draw - `long`, `plan`, or `cross:N`
          
          [default: long]

      --size <SIZE>
          With `--svg`: the drawing's size in pixels, `WIDTHxHEIGHT`
          
          [default: 1200x600]

      --time-factor <FACTOR>
          With `--svg`: metres of depth per unit of time, for objects in time

      --png <FILE.png>
          With `--svg`: the same drawing as a PNG too (needs a build with `--features png`; refused by name otherwise)

      --png-scale <PNG_SCALE>
          With `--png`: how many pixels per pixel of the SVG (2: sharp on a phone)
          
          [default: 2]

      --labels <LABELS>
          With `--svg`: how objects are named - `full` (their titles) or `codes` (`W0`, `H1`, `F2`… and a legend beside the drawing)
          
          [default: full]

      --static
          With `--svg`: write a plain, static SVG. By default the file carries a small script that makes it zoom (wheel), pan (drag) and reset (double click) when opened alone in a browser, with lines that keep their pixel width; without the script the drawing is the same. A redraw (`--from-svg`) keeps what its own metadata says

      --strata-legend
          With `--svg`: a legend of the stratigraphic units the drawn wells show, on the left of the drawing, in a group of its own (`strata-legend`, an Inkscape layer) that is easy to move. Said in a note, never drawn empty, when no well shows a unit. A redraw (`--from-svg`) keeps what its own metadata says

      --strata-ticks
          With `--svg`: a short black tick across each well, wherever one unit gives way to the next (wells coloured by strata), in a group of its own inside the well's. A redraw (`--from-svg`) keeps what its own metadata says

      --hide-unstratified
          With `--svg`: do not draw the portions of a well that carry no strata information (wells coloured by strata): a well is drawn only where a unit is known, and a note counts the wells that lost portions. By default the whole depth is drawn

      --unstratified <STYLE[:PARAM=VALUE,…]>
          With `--svg`: how the portions of a well with no strata information are drawn (wells coloured by strata) - `solid`, `dashed`, `hatched` or `hidden`, with parameters, e.g. `dashed:colour=#999999,dash=6,gap=4` or `hatched:spacing=5,angle=45`. A parameter left out takes its default; the default style is the solid grey a drawing always had. With a style of its own and `--strata-legend`, the legend says what it is. `--hide-unstratified` is `hidden`, and wins

      --marker <NAME:PARAM=VALUE,…>
          With `--svg`: a named marker on the objects of the section whose qualified type contains `type` (`A|B`: any) and whose title contains `title`, case ignored - `NAME:shape=diamond,colour=#1565c0,at=bottom,type=WellboreTrajectory,title=BSS`. `shape` is a RESQML node symbol or `contour`; `at` is `head`, `bottom` or `md` with `md=VALUE`; `size` is in pixels. Repeatable; listed in the legend of markers. A redraw (`--from-svg`) keeps what its own metadata says

      --fill <down|up|both>
          With `--svg`: fill from every surface that may be filled, in its own colour - `down` to the next line below, `up` to the next above, or `both`. Which surfaces may (a horizon, never a fault nor an IJK grid) and where each fill stops are the library's, as on the page's fill buttons. A redraw (`--from-svg`) keeps what its own metadata says

      --hide-notes
          With `--svg`: leave out what the drawing says about itself under its plot (refused objects, wells set aside, labels folded). The command still prints every refusal and note

      --lenient
          Read parts that break the schema instead of refusing them.
          
          Two kinds of defect are read past. ## `energyml select`

```text
Select the objects of a package that fall in a region drawn by outer and inner rings: a list of uuids or uris to chain into an operation

Usage: energyml select [OPTIONS] <FILE>

Arguments:
  <FILE>
          The EPC file

Options:
      --type <TYPE>
          Only objects whose qualified type contains this, case ignored (`WellboreTrajectory`). Repeatable: any of them. With neither `--type` nor a list, every object that has a geometry is judged

      --uuids <U1,U2>
          The objects to judge, by uuid or uri, comma separated

      --from-list <FILE>
          The objects to judge, one uuid or uri per line (blank lines and `#` ignored)

      --outer <FILE.geojson|PACKAGE.epc#UUID>
          A ring a node must be inside one of (none given: everywhere). Either a GeoJSON file - each Polygon's first ring counts as an outer ring of this option and its holes as inner rings - or `PACKAGE.epc#UUID`, a closed polyline of a package, whose system is then the object's

      --inner <FILE.geojson|PACKAGE.epc#UUID>
          A ring a node must be inside none of. Same forms; a Polygon's first ring is the inner ring, and a Polygon with holes is refused (a hole of an inner ring would put an area back, which a region cannot say)

          [default: uuid]

## `energyml import`

```text
Read a GeoJSON and write the EnergyML objects it describes

Usage: energyml import [OPTIONS] <FILE>

Arguments:
  <FILE>
          The GeoJSON file

Options:
      --plan
          Say what the import would make, and write nothing

      --out <OUT>
          Write the result to this EPC

      --into <INTO>
          An existing package to import into. Without it, a new one is made

      --stage <STAGE>
          The stage the export was asked about - what decides top from bottom.
          
          Read off the file name when it follows `GeologicUnit_<Stage>`, and required otherwise.

      --epsg <EPSG>
          The EPSG code the file's coordinates are in. A GeoJSON is WGS 84 by definition (RFC 7946), so 4326 unless you know otherwise
          
          [default: 4326]

      --project <PROJECT>
          Reproject into this EPSG system, in metres.
          
          **Without it the degrees are written as they stand**, which loses nothing and cannot be drawn: the horizontal extent is then in degrees and the vertical in metres, so a 3D view plots a needle - measured at 335:1 on the SIGEOL exports. Nothing in the file lets a reader reconcile the two, so a scene that is to be looked at needs this.
          
          `2154` is Lambert-93, `3949` the CC49 zone the BRGM pipeline writes.

      --vertical-epsg <VERTICAL_EPSG>
          The EPSG code of the vertical system, when it is known.
          
          Left out, the package says **unknown** rather than implying a datum: RFC 7946 means height above the WGS 84 ellipsoid, and a French producer usually writes NGF-IGN69 - forty metres apart, both plausible.

      --data-file <DATA_FILE>
          The external file the coordinates go into
          
          [default: import.h5]

      --originator <ORIGINATOR>
          Who is writing, for every `Citation`
          
          [default: energyml-rust]

      --now <NOW>
          The instant to stamp, `YYYY-MM-DDThh:mm:ssZ`. Defaults to now.
          
          Exposed because it is an **input**: two runs with the same stated time write the same package, byte for byte, which is what makes an import reproducible and diffable.

      --lenient
          Read parts that break the schema instead of refusing them.
          
          Two kinds of defect are read past. ## `energyml create`

```text
Create objects through one door: list what an input allows, plan it, write it

Usage: energyml create [OPTIONS] [OPERATION]

Arguments:
  [OPERATION]
          The operation to run - `energyml create --list` names them

Options:
      --from <[SLOT=]FILE | [SLOT=]FILE.epc#UUID>
          An input: a GeoJSON file, or an object of a package as `model.epc#<uuid>` - its geometry, with the CRS and interpretation it already has. Left out, the operation takes nothing.
          
          Prefixed by `<slot>=`, it goes into that slot of the operation: `--from top=model.epc#<uuid> --from base=model.epc#<uuid>`. An operation with two roles reads them by that name, and without it the piece is named after the object or the file.

      --list
          List what can be created from the input, and what each operation asks

      --json
          With `--list`: print what the operations declare as JSON on stdout, and nothing else - an array of every operation, or one object when an operation is named (`energyml create --list --json contacts-from-frames`). Each carries `name`, `describe`, `makes`, `recipe`, `category`, `also`, `needs` and `takes` (slots: need, default, choices, bounds, cardinality, `applies`, `group`, `about`), `reports` and `gives` (what it writes, by role). Declared on the empty bag, so no input is read: `--from` is ignored

      --set <NAME=VALUE>
          A choice, `name=value`. A number, `true`/`false`, or text

      --plan
          Say what the operation would make, and write nothing

      --out <FILE.epc>
          Write the result to this EPC

      --manifest <FILE.json>
          Write the run manifest to this JSON file: what each step wrote, by role, with the full uris and the collection of the role - what a workflow chains on (`energyml-run-outputs/1`). Needs `--out`: a run that wrote nothing has no outputs to list

      --into <FILE.epc>
          An existing package to add to. Without it, a new one is made

      --template <FILE.json>
          What the columns of the `--from` tables mean: an OSDU `ColumnBasedTableTemplate`, a `File.TabularData`, or the bare list of column definitions.
          
          One template for every table given, which is what a set of files exported by one producer has - the front end applies the first loaded one to every CSV for the same reason. A table given without it is refused naming this flag: what a column means is not something to guess.

      --originator <ORIGINATOR>
          Who is writing, for every `Citation`
          
          [default: energyml-rust]

      --now <NOW>
          The instant to stamp, `YYYY-MM-DDThh:mm:ssZ`. Defaults to now - exposed because it is an input: two runs with the same stated time write the same package, byte for byte

      --recipe <RECIPE.toml>
          Play a recipe: every step, in order, into one package - `--out` to write it, `--plan` to say what it would make. The recipe states its operations, inputs, instant and author, so it takes none of the other options

      --without <GROUP>
          With `--recipe`: leave out the steps of this group (`groupe` in the recipe) - `--without erreur` plays Lutetia without its `[ERROR]` model. Repeat for several

      --lenient
          Read parts that break the schema instead of refusing them.
          
          Two kinds of defect are read past. An absent required element comes back as its default; a value that is *there* and unreadable - a word outside a closed enumeration, a number that is not a number, an undefined entity, an `xsi:type` naming an unknown subtype of a concrete base - is replaced, and the string that was in the file is reported.
          
          Every one of them is reported. Use it to get at the contents of a package whose producer wrote something wrong; do not use it for anything that will be written back, since what comes out is not what the document said.
          
          Still refused in both modes: malformed XML, bad encoding, and an `xsi:type` on a purely abstract choice - there is nothing to fall back to there.

      --strict
          Refuse a part that omits something the schema requires.
          
          By default an absent required element is filled with its default and reported, because refusing costs every field the part *did* carry - a package whose producer left out `Citation.Originator` is otherwise unreadable in its entirety, geometry included.
          
          Use this when the objects will be **written back**: read tolerantly, they hold values nobody wrote, and saving puts those on disk.

      --h5 <[NAME=]PATH>
          An HDF5 file to read arrays from, whatever the package says.
          
          Repeatable, and **the name is optional**:
          
          - `--h5 path/to/data.h5` offers the file without naming it. Offers are opened in the order given and the first that holds the dataset wins. - `--h5 model.h5=path/to/renamed.h5` pins a path to the name the document uses, for when you know which name is wrong.

          What is offered is tried **before** what the package names, since offering one is an explicit instruction and people offer them precisely when the package is wrong. Anything read from somewhere the document did not point at is reported.

      --log <FILTER>
          Show what the operations are doing, on stderr: `info`, `debug`, or a filter such as `energyml_build=debug,energyml_storage=info`.
          
          Nothing is shown by default. The same as the `ENERGYML_LOG` environment variable, which this flag overrides. Spans say how long each step took (`time.busy`). stdout is never touched, so a script reading a result is not disturbed.

      --log-format <FORMAT>
          How `--log` writes a line: `text` (default) or `json`, one object per line. Overrides `ENERGYML_LOG_FORMAT`
          
          [possible values: text, json]

      --strict
          Refuse a part that omits something the schema requires.
          
          By default an absent required element is filled with its default and reported, because refusing costs every field the part *did* carry - a package whose producer left out `Citation.Originator` is otherwise unreadable in its entirety, geometry included.
          
          Use this when the objects will be **written back**: read tolerantly, they hold values nobody wrote, and saving puts those on disk.

      --h5 <[NAME=]PATH>
          An HDF5 file to read arrays from, whatever the package says.
          
          Repeatable, and **the name is optional**:
          
          - `--h5 path/to/data.h5` offers the file without naming it. Offers are opened in the order given and the first that holds the dataset wins. - `--h5 model.h5=path/to/renamed.h5` pins a path to the name the document uses, for when you know which name is wrong.
          
          The name is optional because the whole point is not having to open a `.rels` in a text editor to find out what your file used to be called. A file that was renamed still holds every number it held before.
          
          What is offered is tried **before** what the package names, since offering one is an explicit instruction and people offer them precisely when the package is wrong. Anything read from somewhere the document did not point at is reported.

      --log <FILTER>
          Show what the operations are doing, on stderr: `info`, `debug`, or a filter such as `energyml_build=debug,energyml_storage=info`.
          
          Nothing is shown by default. The same as the `ENERGYML_LOG` environment variable, which this flag overrides. Spans say how long each step took (`time.busy`). stdout is never touched, so a script reading a result is not disturbed.

      --log-format <FORMAT>
          How `--log` writes a line: `text` (default) or `json`, one object per line. Overrides `ENERGYML_LOG_FORMAT`
          
          [possible values: text, json]

  -h, --help
          Print help (see a summary with '-h')
```
